16 — .NET Deep Dive

Scope: the runtime beneath your code. Written for someone who ships ASP.NET Core daily and wants to reason about memory, allocation, JIT, and hosting rather than guess.

1. The runtime

flowchart LR
    CS[C# source] --> ROS[Roslyn compiler]
    ROS --> IL["IL + metadata (.dll)"]
    IL --> LOAD[Assembly load]
    LOAD --> JIT["Tiered JIT<br/>Tier0 fast → Tier1 optimised<br/>(or ReadyToRun / NativeAOT)"]
    JIT --> NATIVE[Native code]
    NATIVE --> EXEC[Execution]
    EXEC <--> GC[Garbage collector]
    EXEC <--> TP[Thread pool]

1.1 JIT and tiering

  • Tier 0 compiles fast with minimal optimisation so startup is quick.
  • After ~30 calls (or a loop's OSR trigger), Tier 1 recompiles with full optimisation using observed profile data (dynamic PGO, on by default since .NET 8 — it devirtualises interface calls and guards hot branches based on real behaviour).
  • ReadyToRun (R2R) pre-compiles to native at publish time: faster startup, slightly lower peak throughput (it's rejitted at Tier 1 for hot paths anyway).
  • NativeAOT: fully ahead-of-time, no JIT, no runtime codegen. Startup in single-digit ms, small memory, small deployment. ⚠️ No reflection-emit, limited reflection, no dynamic assembly loading — so many ORMs, serializers with runtime codegen, and DI containers need source-generator variants. Great for CLI tools, functions, and minimal APIs; check library compatibility first.

Practical impact: benchmark warm, not cold. A microbenchmark that measures Tier 0 code is meaningless — that's why BenchmarkDotNet has a warmup phase.

1.2 Value vs reference types

Reference type (class)                  Value type (struct)
┌──────────┐        ┌──────────────┐    ┌────────────────────┐
│ variable │───────▶│ heap object  │    │ variable holds the │
│ (8 bytes │        │ header 8B    │    │ data inline        │
│  pointer)│        │ MT ptr 8B    │    └────────────────────┘
└──────────┘        │ fields...    │     Stack, inline in an array,
                    └──────────────┘     or inline in a containing object
class struct
Allocation Heap, GC-tracked Inline (stack, array slot, or field)
Copy semantics Reference copied Whole value copied
Overhead 16 bytes header (x64) + fields Exactly its fields (+ padding)
Equality default Reference Structural (but slow via reflection unless you override or use record struct)
Nullability Naturally nullable Nullable<T> wrapper
Best for Entities with identity, large objects, polymorphism Small (≤ ~16–24 bytes), immutable, short-lived values

Rules:

  • readonly record struct for small value objects (Money, PortfolioId, Weight) — no allocation, structural equality, immutability, all free.
  • ⚠️ Large mutable structs are a trap: every assignment and every method call copies the whole thing. A 200-byte struct passed through five layers is 1 KB of copying per call.
  • Boxing silently allocates: assigning a struct to object, to a non-generic interface, or using it in a non-generic collection. int in a List<object>, string.Format("{0}", intValue), or an IComparable cast on a struct all box. Use generics with constraints to avoid it.

1.3 The stack, the heap, and lifetimes

  • Stack: per-thread, ~1 MB default, LIFO, automatically reclaimed. Holds locals, parameters, and value-type data not captured by a closure.
  • Heap: GC-managed. class instances, boxed values, arrays, closures, and async state machines (when they suspend).
  • ⚠️ Closures allocate. A lambda capturing a local creates a display class on the heap. Inside a hot loop, that's an allocation per iteration. Use static lambdas (static x => ..., C# 9+) to force a compile error if you accidentally capture.

2. Garbage collection — enough to diagnose problems

2.1 Generational model

Gen 0 ──survives──▶ Gen 1 ──survives──▶ Gen 2 (long-lived)
 (small, collected very often, very cheap)      (expensive, avoid triggering)

LOH (Large Object Heap): objects ≥ 85,000 bytes → allocated directly, collected with Gen 2,
                          NOT compacted by default (fragmentation!)
POH (Pinned Object Heap): pinned buffers, .NET 5+, keeps pins out of the normal heaps

The generational hypothesis: most objects die young. So collecting only Gen 0 (a small region) reclaims most garbage for a fraction of the cost.

Allocation is ~free — a pointer bump in the allocation context. Collection is the cost, and it scales with the number of surviving objects, not the number allocated. This inverts the intuition: allocating 1M short-lived objects is cheap; keeping 100k objects alive across generations is expensive.

2.2 GC flavours

Mode Behaviour Use
Workstation One heap, tuned for latency on a client Desktop apps
Server (<ServerGarbageCollection>true) One heap + one GC thread per core, higher throughput Server workloads — default for ASP.NET Core
Concurrent/Background Gen 2 collected mostly in the background On by default; reduces pause times
GCHeapHardLimit Caps the heap (container-aware: 75% of the limit) Containers
TieredPGO, DATAS .NET 8+: dynamic adaptation of heap count to load Reduces memory in low-load containers

2.3 Diagnosing memory problems

Symptom Likely cause Investigate
Steady growth, no plateau Leak — something roots objects dotnet-gcdump → compare two snapshots → look at the retention path
High Gen 2 / LOH, frequent full GCs Large or long-lived allocations Reduce allocation, pool buffers, GCSettings.LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode occasionally
High CPU in GC Excessive allocation rate dotnet-counters → gc-heap-size, alloc-rate, time-in-gc (> ~10% is a problem)
Latency spikes Gen 2 pauses / LOH fragmentation Background GC, allocation reduction, ArrayPool
OOM in a container Heap limit vs container limit mismatch Compare GCHeapHardLimit with the cgroup limit

The classic .NET leaks:

  1. Static collections that only grow (a cache with no eviction).
  2. Event handlers never unsubscribed — the publisher roots the subscriber.
  3. Timers and CancellationTokenRegistration not disposed.
  4. Captured this in a long-lived lambda or Task.
  5. HttpClient per request (socket exhaustion, not strictly a memory leak, but the same class of resource bug).
  6. IDisposable not disposed — file handles, connections, SemaphoreSlim, CancellationTokenSource.
dotnet-counters monitor -p <pid> System.Runtime
dotnet-gcdump collect -p <pid>           # then diff two dumps in Visual Studio / PerfView
dotnet-trace collect -p <pid> --profile gc-verbose

2.4 Allocation reduction toolkit

// 1. Span/Memory: slice without copying
ReadOnlySpan<char> code = line.AsSpan(0, 12);            // no substring allocation
if (code.SequenceEqual("GB0009252882")) { ... }

// 2. ArrayPool for large, short-lived buffers
byte[] buffer = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(64 * 1024);
try { /* use buffer.AsSpan(0, length) */ }
finally { ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Return(buffer); }        // MUST return, ideally in finally

// 3. stackalloc for small, known-size scratch space
Span<byte> hash = stackalloc byte[32];
SHA256.HashData(input, hash);

// 4. string.Create to build a string in one allocation
var id = string.Create(16, portfolioId, (span, value) => value.TryFormat(span, out _));

// 5. Struct enumerators — foreach over List<T> typed as List<T> allocates nothing;
//    typed as IEnumerable<T> it boxes the enumerator.

// 6. ValueTask for hot paths that usually complete synchronously (cache hits)
public ValueTask<Quote> GetAsync(string symbol) =>
    _cache.TryGetValue(symbol, out var q) ? new ValueTask<Quote>(q) : new ValueTask<Quote>(LoadAsync(symbol));

// 7. Source-generated JSON and logging — no reflection, no boxing
[JsonSerializable(typeof(PortfolioResponse))]
internal sealed partial class AppJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext;

[LoggerMessage(Level = LogLevel.Information,
    Message = "Portfolio {PortfolioId} rebalanced with {TradeCount} trades")]
static partial void LogRebalanced(ILogger logger, int portfolioId, int tradeCount);

⚠️ Optimise allocations only where you've measured them. Most application code should be written for clarity; the runtime handles gen-0 garbage extremely well. Reach for this toolkit in parsing loops, serialization, and per-request hot paths.

3. ASP.NET Core

3.1 The pipeline

Kestrel (or IIS/HTTP.sys)
  → middleware 1 → middleware 2 → ... → routing → endpoint (controller/minimal API)
  ← response flows back out through the same middleware in reverse

Order is the configuration. The canonical order:

app.UseExceptionHandler();          // outermost: catches everything below
app.UseHsts();
app.UseHttpsRedirection();
app.UseForwardedHeaders();          // BEFORE anything that reads scheme/IP (see file 01 §8.2)
app.UseStaticFiles();               // short-circuit before auth for public assets
app.UseRouting();                   // decides the endpoint
app.UseCors();
app.UseRateLimiter();
app.UseAuthentication();            // who
app.UseAuthorization();             // what — MUST be after UseRouting
app.UseResponseCompression();
app.MapControllers();

⚠️ Getting UseAuthorization before UseRouting, or UseForwardedHeaders after UseHttpsRedirection, produces subtle, environment-specific bugs (redirect loops, endpoints with no authorisation metadata).

3.2 Dependency injection

Lifetime Instance per Watch
Transient Every resolution Disposables accumulate until the scope ends
Scoped Request DbContext lives here
Singleton Process Must be thread-safe; never capture a scoped service 
// Catch captive dependencies and missing registrations at startup, in every environment
builder.Host.UseDefaultServiceProvider((ctx, options) =>
{
    options.ValidateScopes  = true;
    options.ValidateOnBuild = true;
});

// Keyed services (.NET 8+) replace many hand-written factories
builder.Services.AddKeyedScoped<IExporter, PdfExporter>("pdf");
public sealed class ReportController([FromKeyedServices("pdf")] IExporter exporter) { }

3.3 Configuration & options

builder.Services.AddOptions<PricingOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection(PricingOptions.SectionName))
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .Validate(o => o.TimeoutSeconds is > 0 and <= 60, "Timeout must be between 1 and 60 seconds.")
    .ValidateOnStart();        // fail at startup, not on the first request at 3am
Interface Lifetime Reloads?
IOptions<T> Singleton No — snapshot at first use
IOptionsSnapshot<T> Scoped Per request
IOptionsMonitor<T> Singleton Yes, with change callbacks

3.4 Minimal APIs vs controllers

Minimal APIs: less ceremony, better startup, NativeAOT-friendly, ideal for small services and internal endpoints. Controllers: model binding conventions, filters, [ApiController] behaviours, better for large surface areas with shared cross-cutting concerns. Both are first-class; pick per project and be consistent.

3.5 Filters, middleware, and where to put cross-cutting logic

Need Use
Applies to all requests including static files Middleware
Needs the endpoint/model Action filter / endpoint filter
Needs the result before serialisation Result filter
Applies to a use case, not HTTP A pipeline behaviour (MediatR) or a decorator
Exception → HTTP mapping IExceptionHandler (.NET 8) or UseExceptionHandler

3.6 Health checks and graceful shutdown

builder.Services.AddHealthChecks()
    .AddDbContextCheck<AppDbContext>("db", tags: ["ready"])
    .AddRedis(redisCs, name: "cache", failureStatus: HealthStatus.Degraded, tags: ["ready"]);

app.MapHealthChecks("/health/live",  new() { Predicate = _ => false });                 // process alive
app.MapHealthChecks("/health/ready", new() { Predicate = c => c.Tags.Contains("ready") });

builder.Services.Configure<HostOptions>(o => o.ShutdownTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));

⚠️ A readiness check that hard-fails on a shared dependency takes the whole fleet out of rotation during a blip (file 02 §3.4). Prefer Degraded for optional dependencies.

4. EF Core internals

4.1 The pipeline

LINQ expression tree → query translation (provider) → SQL → ADO.NET → DbDataReader
                                                                   → materialisation → change tracker

Change tracker: for each tracked entity, EF keeps a snapshot and compares on SaveChanges. This is why:

  • Tracking large read-only result sets is wasteful → AsNoTracking().
  • SaveChanges cost scales with the number of tracked entities, not the number changed.
  • Sharing a DbContext across threads corrupts it — the tracker is not thread-safe.

4.2 The performance rules

// Read path: no tracking, project to a DTO, bounded
var page = await db.Trades.AsNoTracking()
    .Where(t => t.PortfolioId == id && t.TradeDate >= from)
    .OrderByDescending(t => t.TradeDate).ThenByDescending(t => t.Id)
    .Select(t => new TradeDto(t.Id, t.InstrumentCode, t.Notional, t.TradeDate))
    .Take(100)
    .ToListAsync(ct);

// Bulk update without loading entities (EF 7+)
await db.Trades.Where(t => t.Status == TradeStatus.Stale)
    .ExecuteUpdateAsync(s => s.SetProperty(t => t.Status, TradeStatus.Archived), ct);

// Split query when Includes cause a cartesian explosion
var portfolio = await db.Portfolios
    .Include(p => p.Holdings).Include(p => p.Benchmarks)
    .AsSplitQuery()
    .FirstOrDefaultAsync(p => p.Id == id, ct);
Rule Why
AsNoTracking() on reads Skips snapshot creation and identity resolution
Project with Select Fetch only needed columns; avoids over-fetch and lazy-load traps
AsSplitQuery() for multiple collection Includes Avoids row multiplication (one 3×4 join = 12 rows of duplicated parent data)
ExecuteUpdate/ExecuteDelete One statement instead of load-modify-save
AddDbContextPool Reuses context instances in high-throughput APIs
Compiled queries Skips expression-tree translation on hot paths
Never lazy loading in a request path It's how N+1 becomes invisible
Read the generated SQL The gap between intent and emitted SQL is where the time goes 
// Development only — see exactly what EF emits
if (builder.Environment.IsDevelopment())
    options.EnableSensitiveDataLogging().LogTo(Console.WriteLine, LogLevel.Information);

4.3 Concurrency and transactions

// Optimistic concurrency
modelBuilder.Entity<Portfolio>().Property(p => p.RowVersion).IsRowVersion();

try { await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct); }
catch (DbUpdateConcurrencyException ex)
{
    // Reload, merge, or surface a 409/412 to the client — never silently overwrite
}

// With EnableRetryOnFailure you MUST wrap manual transactions in the execution strategy
var strategy = db.Database.CreateExecutionStrategy();
await strategy.ExecuteAsync(async () =>
{
    await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);
    // ... work ...
    await tx.CommitAsync(ct);
});

4.4 Migrations discipline

Review the generated SQL every time (dotnet ef migrations script). Auto-generated migrations happily emit a table rebuild that locks a production table for minutes. Expand/contract for anything that runs while old code is still deployed (file 10 §9).

5. Performance measurement

Never optimise without measuring. The order:

  1. Is it actually slow? Check APM p95/p99 for the endpoint, not a hunch.
  2. Where is the time? Distributed trace → is it DB, downstream HTTP, CPU, or waiting?
  3. Profile the suspect.
  4. Change one thing. Re-measure.
dotnet-counters monitor -p <pid> System.Runtime Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting
dotnet-trace collect  -p <pid> --profile cpu-sampling      # → open in PerfView/Speedscope
dotnet-dump  collect  -p <pid>                             # → analyse with dotnet-dump analyze

// BenchmarkDotNet for micro-level decisions — the only credible way to compare two implementations
[MemoryDiagnoser]
[SimpleJob(RuntimeMoniker.Net90)]
public class ParsingBenchmarks
{
    private readonly string _line = "GB0009252882,1000.50,2026-07-27";

    [Benchmark(Baseline = true)]
    public decimal Split() => decimal.Parse(_line.Split(',')[1]);      // allocates a string[]

    [Benchmark]
    public decimal Span()
    {
        var s = _line.AsSpan();
        int first = s.IndexOf(',');
        var rest = s[(first + 1)..];
        return decimal.Parse(rest[..rest.IndexOf(',')]);                // zero allocation
    }
}

⚠️ Never microbenchmark with Stopwatch in a loop — you'll measure JIT tiering, GC timing, and dead-code elimination rather than your code.

Common .NET performance wins, in rough order of impact:

  1. Fix the database (indexes, N+1, over-fetching) — usually 80% of the time.
  2. Remove sync-over-async / thread-pool starvation (file 12 §2.4).
  3. Add caching at the right layer.
  4. Reduce payload size (projection, compression, pagination).
  5. Reduce allocations in hot paths.
  6. Parallelise genuinely CPU-bound work.

6. Modern C# features worth using

Feature Version Use
record / record struct 9/10 DTOs, value objects, immutable models
Pattern matching + switch expressions 8+ Replace type-switch chains; exhaustiveness
Nullable reference types 8 Compile-time null safety. Turn it on
init accessors, required members 9/11 Immutable-after-construction with object initialisers
File-scoped namespaces, global usings 10 Less noise
Primary constructors 12 public sealed class Svc(IRepo repo) — concise DI
Collection expressions 12 [.. items, newItem], List<int> x = [];
Raw string literals 11 SQL and JSON without escaping
LibraryImport, source generators 7+ Compile-time codegen instead of reflection
TimeProvider 8 Testable time — stop using DateTime.Now
System.Threading.Lock 9 Better than lock (object)
FrozenDictionary/FrozenSet 8 Fast read-only lookups
[LoggerMessage] source gen 6+ Allocation-free structured logging 
// Primary constructor + record + pattern matching + collection expression, idiomatic modern C#
public sealed class RebalanceService(IPortfolioRepository repo, TimeProvider clock)
{
    public async Task<Result<IReadOnlyList<Trade>>> RunAsync(PortfolioId id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var portfolio = await repo.LoadAsync(id, ct);
        return portfolio switch
        {
            null                                   => Result.NotFound<IReadOnlyList<Trade>>(id),
            { Status: PortfolioStatus.Frozen }     => Result.Conflict<IReadOnlyList<Trade>>("Portfolio is frozen."),
            { Holdings.Count: 0 }                  => Result.Ok<IReadOnlyList<Trade>>([]),
            var p                                  => Result.Ok(Calculate(p, clock.GetUtcNow()))
        };
    }
}

7. Testing in .NET

Level Tool Note
Unit xUnit + FluentAssertions Pure logic; no mocks needed if the core is pure (file 05 §8)
Mocking NSubstitute / Moq Mock owned abstractions, not third-party types you don't control
Integration WebApplicationFactory<Program> The real pipeline, in-memory server
Database Testcontainers A real SQL Server/Postgres per test run. Never UseInMemoryDatabase — it doesn't enforce constraints, transactions, or SQL semantics, so it passes tests that fail in production
HTTP dependencies WireMock.Net Fake the wire, not the client class
Snapshot Verify Complex outputs, generated files
Property-based FsCheck / CsCheck Invariants over generated inputs
Load k6, NBomber Before you claim it scales
Architecture NetArchTest Enforce layer rules in CI (file 07 §4) 
public sealed class TradesApiTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
    : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task GetTrades_WithoutAuthentication_Returns401()
    {
        var client = factory.CreateClient();
        var response = await client.GetAsync("/api/v1/trades");
        response.StatusCode.Should().Be(HttpStatusCode.Unauthorized);
    }
}

8. Deployment & hosting

Option Startup Ops Use
IIS / Windows Service Slow Manual Existing on-prem estates
Azure App Service Fast Low Standard web apps — the default for many .NET shops
Azure Container Apps Fast Low Containers without k8s
AKS/EKS Fast High Platform teams, many services
Azure Functions Cold-start sensitive Lowest Event-driven, spiky
NativeAOT + container ~5 ms Low CLI, sidecars, scale-to-zero functions

Publish settings worth knowing:

<PropertyGroup>
  <TargetFramework>net9.0</TargetFramework>
  <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
  <InvariantGlobalization>true</InvariantGlobalization>   <!-- smaller image; check your culture needs -->
  <ServerGarbageCollection>true</ServerGarbageCollection>
  <ConcurrentGarbageCollection>true</ConcurrentGarbageCollection>
  <PublishReadyToRun>true</PublishReadyToRun>
</PropertyGroup>

⚠️ InvariantGlobalization changes string comparison and date/number formatting — safe for many APIs, breaking for anything culture-sensitive. Decide deliberately.

9. Observability

builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry()
    .ConfigureResource(r => r.AddService("orders-api", serviceVersion: version))
    .WithTracing(t => t
        .AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation(o => o.RecordException = true)
        .AddHttpClientInstrumentation()
        .AddEntityFrameworkCoreInstrumentation()
        .AddOtlpExporter())
    .WithMetrics(m => m
        .AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation()
        .AddRuntimeInstrumentation()          // GC, thread pool, exceptions
        .AddOtlpExporter());

Structured logging, always:

// ❌ log.LogInformation($"Rebalanced portfolio {id} with {count} trades");   // one opaque string
// ✔ named placeholders → queryable fields in the log store
log.LogInformation("Rebalanced portfolio {PortfolioId} with {TradeCount} trades", id, count);

Details in file 23.

10. Checklist & interview angles

.NET production checklist

  • Nullable reference types on; warnings as errors
  • ServerGarbageCollection enabled for server workloads
  • No .Result/.Wait(); CancellationToken threaded through
  • IHttpClientFactory with timeouts, PooledConnectionLifetime, and resilience
  • DI scopes validated at startup; no captive dependencies
  • Options validated with ValidateOnStart
  • EF: AsNoTracking on reads, projections, no lazy loading, SQL reviewed
  • Health checks split live/ready; shutdown timeout > longest request
  • OpenTelemetry traces + metrics + structured logs with correlation
  • TimeProvider injected instead of DateTime.Now
  • Integration tests on a real database (Testcontainers)
  • Load tested; GC counters and thread-pool queue observed under load

🔍 Interview angles

  • Value vs reference type — when do you use a struct? Small, immutable, short-lived values where allocation matters; beware copying cost and boxing.
  • Explain the generational GC. Most objects die young, so collecting Gen 0 reclaims most garbage cheaply; survivors are promoted; Gen 2 and LOH collections are expensive, so the goal is to avoid surviving, not to avoid allocating.
  • What's on the LOH and why does it matter? Objects ≥ 85 KB; collected with Gen 2 and not compacted by default → fragmentation and long pauses. Pool large buffers instead.
  • How does async/await work? The compiler builds a state machine; await on incomplete work registers a continuation and returns the thread; completion resumes it. No thread is held during I/O.
  • IEnumerable vs IQueryable? In-memory iteration vs an expression tree translated by a provider. Calling AsEnumerable()/ToList() too early moves filtering from the database into your process.
  • How do you find a memory leak? Two gcdumps under steady load, diff them, inspect the retention path of the growing type. Then look for statics, events, timers, and captured closures.
  • Singleton vs scoped vs transient — what breaks? Capturing a scoped DbContext in a singleton shares it across requests and threads: corrupted change tracker, random exceptions. ValidateScopes catches it.
  • Minimal API or controllers? Either; choose by surface size and cross-cutting needs, and be consistent within a service.
